title.value: A Place Further Than the Universe

logline: Four high school girls embark on an Antarctic expedition together - one driven by grief over a missing mother, the others by restlessness, loneliness, and a hunger for something that actually matters.

renewal.note: The 13-episode original anime by Madhouse aired from January to March 2018 and concluded as a complete standalone story. No sequel has been produced or announced.

bollymeter.basis: MAL score of 8.50 from a large voting base; Anime News Network episode reviewers consistently praised the series for its emotional architecture, with ANN user weighted mean at 8.40 (Very Good+) and 86 votes of Masterpiece.

pull_quotes.text: It's been able to achieve its modest narrative ambitions without any trouble, and that foundation should give it plenty to build on.

seasons.review_body: Madhouse's original 2018 anime - broadcast on AT-X and Tokyo MX - is widely considered one of the finest anime of that decade. Directed by Atsuko Ishizuka and written by Jukki Hanada, the series uses the Antarctic expedition as both a literal and emotional destination. The four leads are distinct and credibly teenage; their reasons for attempting something this extreme are grounded in recognisable adolescent longing rather than fantasy. Anime News Network's episodic reviewers tracked the series' slow emotional build across 13 weeks, consistently noting how the show layers meaning into its visual design and character dynamics before delivering its most emotionally powerful episodes. The finale is among the most discussed in recent anime history. The series earned simulcast status on Crunchyroll and won the Anime of the Year award at the Crunchyroll Anime Awards in 2019.

episode_reviews.title: One Million Yen Worth of Youth
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: Mari Tamaki has lived a life of almost-adventures and abandoned dreams. When she meets Shirase Kobuchizawa, who has spent years saving a million yen to reach Antarctica, the premise snaps into focus immediately. The premiere is warm, propulsive, and confidently specific.
episode_reviews.the_moment: A million yen spilling from a bag - the most concrete expression of years of single-minded resolve any anime premiere has offered.
episode_reviews.review_body:
# A Place Further Than The Universe S01E01: "One Million Yen Worth of Youth" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

**Kimari** starts with a nightmare about her mother trying to kill her with a wet towel. It is ridiculous, blunt, and exactly the right doorway into a premiere about fear wearing silly clothes. The fear here is ordinary and embarrassing. High school is passing by, and Kimari remains the girl who almost does something.

She wants an aimless trip, chooses Tokyo, prepares to run away alone, and still needs the story to push her into motion. The episode works because it treats youth less like freedom than a muscle that has to be forced awake. That gives the premiere its cleanest tension. Kimari is surrounded by chances to move, yet she cannot make movement mean anything until someone else's impossible plan gives her restlessness a shape.

## Youth Begins as an Excuse

The smartest thing in "One Million Yen Worth of Youth" is that Kimari's first dream of rebellion is vague. She does not begin with a mission. She begins with discomfort. the episode frames her high school action plan as an aimless journey to Tokyo, a lovely small target for a character who wants the feeling of decisiveness without carrying the burden of a reason.

That choice matters. A weaker premiere would hand Kimari a grand destiny in minute one and ask the viewer to applaud her courage. This one starts with avoidance. She prepares to run away alone, riding away from school life as if distance itself can become personality. The run has romance in it, along with embarrassment. Tokyo is close enough to be practical and far enough to sound brave in a teenage diary.

The episode's early quiet stretches help that contradiction land. Before the dialogue grows dense, the hour gives Kimari room to feel the weight of staying put. The silence does not turn her into a tragic figure. It makes her ordinary, which is better. Her problem is that she knows paths exist and has no idea which one she can claim without lying to herself.

Her attempted escape also exposes how much performance sits inside her fantasy. She wants proof that she is capable of doing something reckless. The destination matters less than the evidence. That is why the plan feels fragile from the start. Kimari is trying to manufacture a version of herself, and the episode lets that effort look small without mocking her for it.

That is why her later pivot into helping matters. Kimari does not complete the original fantasy alone. She changes her story, calls the school, and chooses support over solo performance. The premiere's first argument is clean: courage may start as escape, then become useful once it attaches itself to someone else's impossible plan.

## The Million Yen Gives Restlessness a Shape

The one million yen is the episode's cleverest object because it makes aimlessness impossible. Money has weight. Money has an owner. Money creates a trail. By the time characters are searching freshmen rooms and wondering whether the girl they want is there, the episode has shifted from Kimari's soft fantasy into something with consequence.

That search beat is partly mechanical. It exists to connect Kimari's drifting energy to **Kobuchizawa Shirase**, and the writing does not hide the machinery. A girl is being looked for. The money started the search. The question of who dropped it and how it connects to Kobuchizawa becomes one of the premiere's open loops. The construction is visible, yet effective, because the title has already told the viewer what the hour is buying: youth with a price tag.

The yen works because it embarrasses everyone around it. Kimari's Tokyo plan is all mood. Kobuchizawa's money suggests work, obsession, and risk. The object exposes the gap between wanting to go somewhere and preparing to go somewhere. The premiere never has to lecture that difference. It simply places Kimari beside a person whose desire has been converted into cash, effort, and a trail other people can follow.

That contrast gives the episode a useful jolt. Kimari can fantasize about escape because her plan has almost no cost. Kobuchizawa's plan has already demanded something from her. The money makes that demand visible. It turns private grief into an object that can be lost, found, questioned, and misunderstood.

The flaw is that the middle stretch grows explain-y once the plot needs everyone in position. The frequent turn-taking keeps the information legible, though a little more friction in the search itself would have sharpened the mystery. The episode is at its best when action reveals character. Here, a few beats announce the bridge while building it.

## Antarctica Enters Like a Dare

Kobuchizawa's story changes the scale of the episode in one sentence. Her mother wrote about Antarctica, went there, went missing, and was never found. Kobuchizawa's response is plain: "So, I'm going to find her." The line is almost absurd in its simplicity, and the episode knows it. Antarctica is not Tokyo. It is not a school-skipping stunt. It is a place far enough away that the dream sounds like self-punishment to anyone listening.

This is where the premiere finds its spine. Kimari wants motion because stillness scares her. Kobuchizawa wants Antarctica because grief has turned into direction. One girl is trying to become someone. The other has already decided what she must do, even if every surrounding voice treats the plan as impossible.

The central skepticism is important. The hour keeps returning to the basic question of whether Antarctica is possible, and Kobuchizawa has to live inside that disbelief. Her contradiction drives the episode: she explains the hardship and the doubts, then pushes others to come see the ship anyway. She is dragging the fantasy toward proof.

That makes her compelling without making her easy. She has a goal so fixed that it can crowd out ordinary conversation. The dialogue around her becomes dense because she carries too much backstory and too much intent for a casual scene. Still, the force of the desire cuts through. When Kobuchizawa enters fully, the premiere stops being about skipping school and starts being about the nerve it takes to say the impossible out loud.

The episode also avoids making her grief neat. Kobuchizawa's plan is inspiring because it is unreasonable, and troubling for the same reason. That tension keeps Antarctica from becoming a postcard. The continent functions as distance, proof, and wound. Every time she says where she wants to go, the scale of the claim reminds the room how little sympathy can do for her.

## The Ship Turns Fantasy Into Homework

The final movement is where the episode earns its title's swagger. The announcement that the icebreaker Shirase is open to the public in Kure Port gives Kobuchizawa's Antarctica plan a physical next step. A ship is not a metaphor in the scene. It is an appointment. It has a port, a date, a public opening, and the ability to turn disbelief into logistics.

That is a strong premiere move. Instead of ending on pure yearning, the episode ends on preview. Come next Saturday. Look at the ship. Test the claim with your own feet. The invitation matters because it shifts the story from private obsession into shared possibility. Kimari, who began by trying to run from school life alone, now has a reason to move with someone.

The icebreaker being named Shirase adds a sharp echo to Kobuchizawa's presence. The girl and the vessel share the sound of destination. The episode does not need to overplay it. It simply places the name at the point where the dream becomes tangible, and the connection does its quiet work.

There is also a nice tonal acceleration here. The early quiet stretches give way to plans, explanations, and invitations. That movement mirrors Kimari's own awakening. The premiere begins with her trapped in the comedy of fear, then ends with her standing near a goal large enough to make fear useful. The hour has not solved the Antarctica problem. It has made the next step impossible to ignore.

The ship also clarifies the show's promise. This story will need more than yearning, cash, and a dramatic declaration. It will need access, timing, adult systems, and endurance. By ending on a public opening rather than a private vow, the premiere turns adventure into procedure. That sounds dry. It is exactly what the episode needs.

## The Verdict

"One Million Yen Worth of Youth" is a very good premiere because it understands the difference between wanting adventure and earning a reason to leave. Kimari's aimless Tokyo plan gives the episode its relatable restlessness, while Kobuchizawa's Antarctica mission gives it bite, grief, and direction. The one million yen thread is slightly more functional than elegant, and the middle's dense explanations occasionally flatten the mystery. Even so, the hour has a clean dramatic argument: teenage motion gains meaning when it meets purpose.

As a season opener, it plants two strong loops, the owner of the money and the possibility of reaching Antarctica, while making the ship invitation feel like the first concrete step. The premiere is funny, anxious, and purposeful in the right places. Most importantly, it lets Kimari's small fear collide with Kobuchizawa's enormous demand, then trusts that collision to carry the story south.

Written by BollyAI, reviewed by our editorial team.

verdict.one_liner: A sharp premiere that turns Kimari’s vague escape fantasy into Shirase’s impossible, money-staked route south.

episode_reviews.title: A Place Further Than the Universe
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale delivers the emotional payoff the series has been building across 12 episodes. The Antarctic setting, the search for what was lost, and the bonds formed during the journey all converge in a sequence that critics and audiences consistently identify as one of the most affecting in contemporary anime.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The email inbox - a scene described by the ANN reviewer as finally delivering the dramatic bite the series had been building toward.

critic_note.text: This episode finally gave me what I wanted most out of this show: a storyline with some genuine dramatic bite.
